Wed, 22 Apr 2026 07:00:00 GMT,The power grid is breaking. Can it fix itself?,"A week before Christmas, nearly 50,000 people living along Colorado’s Front Range lost power for multiple days.

The outage was deliberate. Xcel Energy, the region’s utility, had implemented a “public safety power shutoff” out of fear that high winds would down power lines and spark fires. The danger wasn’t hypothetical. Conditions were warm and dry, with wind gusts exceeding 100 miles per hour. In 2021, a similar windstorm had led to the most destructive wildfire in Colorado history: the Marshall Fire, which destroyed 1,084 homes in the region.

Given the risk, the December 2025 outage may have been justified, but a grid that must be shut down for multiple days because of high winds — disrupting the lives of tens of thousands of people in the process — points to a deeper problem: America’s power grid is at a breaking point.

To avoid a future plagued by more frequent blackouts, researchers are shifting some of the responsibility for keeping the lights on from utilities to the grid itself with “self-healing” technologies that can detect disruptions, isolate problems, and reroute energy — automatically.
Power grids 101

Much of the infrastructure that makes it so when you flip a switch in your home, the light turns on is hidden, so before we get into how to make the electric grid more resilient, let’s recap how it currently works in the U.S.
Winds forced the utility to preemptively cut off power to nearly 50,000 people. A grid that must be shut down for days because of high winds is a grid at a breaking point.

At a high level, the electric grid consists of three main processes — generation, transmission, and distribution — and electricity moves across them like it’s traveling along a one-way street. First, it is generated at a power plant using coal, natural gas, nuclear fission, or renewables. It then moves across high-voltage transmission lines to substations, where voltage is stepped down. From those, it travels across neighborhood-level distribution lines to homes and businesses.

Electricity moves across the grid in just one direction — from generation to transmission to distribution— but it doesn’t flow across just one route. The grid is a network, with many interconnected lines and substations. This redundancy means that, if one pathway fails, operators can reconfigure the network by opening and closing switches and circuit breakers to redistribute power onto alternate lines. This requires diagnosing conditions and making decisions with incomplete information. While often done remotely, the process still takes minutes to hours, delaying restoration and increasing the risk of cascading failures.
Why the grid fails

The electric grid can fail for multiple reasons, but the most common is physical damage. Imagine a power pole that snaps in the wind. Risks to physical infrastructure include basic equipment failures, damage from wildlife, and extreme weather events, which are becoming more common due to climate change.

Bad actors can also attack physical infrastructure — Russia has launched physical attacks on Ukraine’s energy grid in an attempt to cripple the economy and crush morale. They can also target the digital infrastructure that keeps everything working. According to industry data cited in a report by the International Energy Agency, a typical utility experienced more than 1,500 cyberattacks per week in 2024.
But sometimes, the only thing that needs to happen for the grid to fail is for people to want to use it.
The U.S. power grid is already enormous, yet transmission systems will still need to double or triple by 2050 to reliably meet growing demand.

For the grid to function, energy generation (the amount of energy being produced at power plants) must match demand from end users. Even small imbalances can lead to outages and blackouts. “Most people don’t realize how fragile the grid is to real-time balancing between load and generation,” says Sean Fleming, writer of Clean Energy Review and an expert on how modern power grids are built and maintained. “Electricity is not easily storable, and if supply and demand get out of whack even a bit, equipment can be severely damaged and the whole system can go offline.”

The redundancy built into the grid only goes so far in preventing outages. Because transmission and distribution lines have finite capacity, every route has a capacity limit, and a failure along one pathway can cause others to be overloaded.

When bottlenecks occur, especially if there are multiple failure points, failures can cascade through the system. This can lead to rolling blackouts, where rerouted power overwhelms and brings down each successive pathway. Fleming says that “protection schemes are built into the grid to disconnect equipment or shut down systems when supply and demand don’t match.” These can protect the system, but they also mean outages for consumers.
Why the problem is getting worse
The grid is currently facing new challenges on both the supply and demand sides of the equation.

U.S. electricity demand grew by 2.1% in 2025 and is expected to rise 2% per year through 2030, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA), which projects half of the new demand may come from new data centers. Electrification technologies, such as residential heat pumps and electric vehicles, are good for decarbonization, but they’re also increasing demand at a time when the grid is already stretched thin.
If we want to add new capacity to the grid, we need to build new lines — and not just a few.

At the end of 2024, more than 10,000 generation projects were waiting for grid interconnection. The U.S. power grid is already enormous, with more than 600,000 miles of high voltage transmission lines and more than 6.3 million miles of distribution lines, yet transmission systems will still need to double or triple by 2050 to reliably meet growing demand, according to scenarios modeled in a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) study. If new transmission lines are needed, that means building new infrastructure across vast distances — low cost renewable energy resources are often far from where the energy is needed — a notoriously difficult task due to permitting processes that Congress is debating how to reform.
When you consider the complexity of the task of operating an electric grid, it’s a miracle that the lights stay on at all.
Alexandra “Sascha” von Meier

At the same time, the renewable transition is also creating new challenges. While wind and solar are cleaner than coal and natural gas, they are also less consistent forms of generation, and their use makes supply management less predictable and harder for operators to manage manually.

Distributed resources linked to renewables, such as solar panels and batteries, are also disrupting the linear nature of the grid, adding complexity and more failure points. Instead of electricity flowing in one direction — from power plants to end users — homes and businesses can now generate their own power and return excess energy back to the grid.

This provides more flexibility, but it also means the grid increasingly needs to function more like a two-way street than a one-way street. This is not a function the traditional grid can easily support. To take full advantage of renewables and batteries, the grid will need to move electrons more adaptively in multiple directions.

Dynamic grid management requires knowing exactly how the grid is functioning moment to moment — and that’s more clarity than grid operators typically have. “When you consider the complexity of the task of operating an electric grid, the many different crises that can happen, and the paucity of data traditionally available, it’s a miracle that the lights stay on at all,” says Alexandra “Sascha” von Meier, the former Director of the Electric Grid Research program at the California Institute for Energy and Environment.
Instead of being a static, centrally managed system, the grid is becoming a dynamic, data-driven one that can respond to conditions in real time.
Modernizing the grid

These new challenges to the grid come at a time when it is already in need of updating due to age. Estimates from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) show more than 50% of transformers are more than 33 years old and approaching the end of life. Meanwhile, 70% of transmission lines are 25 years or older. The U.S. is taking steps to update this aging infrastructure, but that will take time. We need to modernize the grid we currently have to handle today’s challenges, and that’s why utilities are moving towards making them self-healing.

“A self-healing grid is a power system that proactively detects disturbances, isolates the problem, and restores service automatically, often in seconds,” says Massoud Amin, the “father of the smart grid” and professor emeritus at the University of Minnesota. “It uses sensors, communications, and advanced controls distributed across the network to monitor the system and take corrective action continuously. The goal is simple: prevent small disturbances from turning into large outages.”

A self-healing grid is not an endpoint. It’s a spectrum of capabilities. Together, they transform the grid from a passive network into an adaptive system that enables utilities to “identify and respond to issues and outages faster and mitigate them in as close to real-time as possible,” says Flemming.

For example, while a self-healing grid can’t automatically repair physical damage — if the wind snaps a power pole, a lineman still needs to go out and repair it — it can detect the problem almost immediately, automatically open and close switches across the network to route power away from the downed line, and stabilize the grid to prevent cascading failures and minimize the area affected by outages. No need to wait for customers to report the downed line.
Investments in self-healing technologies helped Duke Energy Florida avoid 280,000 extended power outages and more than 300,000 hours of outages for customers in 2025.

This is fundamentally different from how the grid has historically operated. Instead of being a static, centrally managed system, the grid is becoming a dynamic, data-driven one that can respond to conditions in real time.

“The traditional grid is largely reactive,” says Amin. “When something fails, equipment trips, and crews respond after the outage occurs. A self-healing grid is aware and adaptive. It senses disturbances in real time, isolates damaged sections, and reroutes power automatically. The difference is speed and intelligence.”

Self-healing capabilities like the above — automated switches that can quickly isolate faults and reroute power — are already being deployed on local distribution grids. Distribution infrastructure is prioritized because it makes up the vast majority of the grid and accounts for most outages. Duke Energy Florida reported that investments in self-healing technologies helped avoid 280,000 extended power outages and more than 300,000 hours of outages for customers in 2025.

Other technological advances are helping modernize the grid by allowing operators to determine the real-time capacity limits of transmission lines — how much electricity they can carry before conductors overheat. Historically, these limits have been static, conservative, and not entirely accurate — how much power a transmission line can actually carry safely varies depending on weather conditions.

In March, PJM Interconnection became the first grid operator to comply with a Federal Energy Regulatory Commission order to adjust transmission line capacity ratings using real-time weather data. PJM now uses sensors and software to collect and analyze weather conditions and forecasts, allowing it to update transmission limits hourly instead of relying on a fixed rating. Research from the DOE’s Idaho National Laboratory suggests that implementing dynamic ratings could increase usable transmission capacity by roughly 10% to 40%.

AI also has a role to play in grid modernization. In 2024, researchers at NREL published a report describing “eGridGPT,” a generative AI model “engineered to virtually support power grid control room operators by assisting in decision-making processes and interpreting the data and models.” PJM is already using AI for interconnection planning to accelerate the connection of new generation resources to the grid, while NextEra Energy and Google Cloud recently announced a collaboration to deploy AI to enhance both field operations and grid management and optimization efforts.
Our security, economy, and quality of life all fundamentally depend on reliable, affordable, and sustainable electricity. When the grid fails, everything else begins to fail with it.
Massoud Amin

However, AI is not a panacea. I asked several experts about AI’s potential role in achieving self-healing grids, and they were united in their belief that AI would not be the ultimate operator of the grid. “[AI] expands the operator’s field of vision,” says Amin, but it’s still up to the human to make the important decisions. In many respects, AI’s real advantage to the grid operator comes down to speed — by quickly analyzing the troves of data collected by sensors across a modern grid, it can help operators make decisions faster.

Ultimately, it’ll be a combination of better sensors and computing capabilities that will meaningfully improve the capacity and resilience of the grid. As these technologies advance, utilities will be able to deploy them on a wider scale and in more contexts — making the grid more resilient for more people.

“Modern society runs on electricity,” says Amin. “Our security, economy, and quality of life all fundamentally depend on reliable, affordable, and sustainable electricity. When the grid fails, everything else begins to fail with it.”",Big Think
Thu, 23 Apr 2026 07:00:00 GMT,There are fixes for AI’s toll on the power grid. Here’s why they’re not happening
column2: CNN Business,"Tech companies charging ahead with artificial intelligence have a problem: AI’s rapid growth is colliding headlong with a finite amount of available energy and computing power.

column1: AI is evolving beyond chatbots and into autonomous AI agents that demand far more computing power and electricity, leaving companies scrambling for more energy. OpenAI recently shuttered its video-generating app Sora, in part because it was gobbling up the company’s computational supplies.

The data centers that make up the backbone of AI technology need loads of energy – both to keep their servers humming and to prevent overheating. But the United States’ electrical grid isn’t exactly up to the task of powering the 21st century economy. It’s old and janky – a loosely connected collection of three grids: East, West and Texas. Experts have long warned that it is outdated and ill-equipped to respond to everything from severe weather to AI’s insatiable new power demand.

“Basically, we have run out of headroom, largely speaking, in the US,” said Ben Hertz-Shargel, an expert on electrification and data centers at energy research firm Wood Mackenzie. “There is a land grab happening, where companies believe that access to more capacity for compute will be necessary to win the future battle over AI services.”

Companies like Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta are ramping up investments in data centers and electricity generation to power new AI models and services, betting that more energy will be needed to keep up with future AI-drive products. OpenAI last year warned the White House of an “electron gap” that puts US leadership in AI at risk, writing that “electrons are the new oil.”
Elon Musk, CEO of xAI, Tesla and SpaceX, said at the World Economic Forum in January that he expects that more chips will be produced than can be turned on because of power constraints.
A Google spokesperson told CNN that the current pace of energy growth is not yet meeting the potential of AI, and that the US needs to go all-in on energy development to keep pace.

Solutions to the power problem exist: increasing renewable energy and battery development, scaling up traditional energy sources like gas and nuclear power, and expanding the current energy grid’s capacity.
But they all face roadblocks, both politically and practically.
Potential solutions

The industry is lobbying at both the state and federal level for policies that accelerate permitting and maintain incentives for private sector investment, and the Trump administration recommended relaxing federal rules and expediting construction permits in an AI action plan last year.
But delivering more electric infrastructure is more easily said than done. The most immediate solution is getting more power out of the current electrical grid, experts said.

Both the Biden and Trump administrations threw federal dollars at ideas to modernize and expand the grid, including “re-conductoring,” which replaces existing transmission lines with ones that have greater capacity, allowing more electrical current to travel through them. It’s faster than building a new transmission line entirely, which could take seven to ten years to complete.

Data center companies are looking for spare power capacity at every electrical utility they can find, “including very non-traditional utilities and cooperatives whose doors have never been knocked on before,” Hertz-Shargel said.

One answer could be renewable energy sources like wind and solar, which are often much cheaper and faster to build than the large turbines that are the backbone of the generators in gas-fired power plants. The manufacturers who build these turbines have their order books filled; current wait times for a new turbine are over five years.

But renewables have faced a one-two punch lately, with longer permitting times from the Trump administration combined with Republicans in Congress ending tax credits that would have made it cheaper to build them.

These changes “definitely killed perfectly good wind and solar projects that would have reduced energy prices,” said Andrew Levitt, a consultant focused on wholesale electricity at research firm Brattle. However, Levitt said he expected to see growth in renewable projects going forward because the sheer demand for electricity is so great.
Looking to batteries and fusion
AI companies are pouring money into futuristic technology like fusion power and fueling the big battery industry in an effort to satisfy their hunger for electricity.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is backing a $5.4 billion nuclear fusion start-up called Helion Energy, which claims it will supply Microsoft with electricity by 2028. Google, likewise, has signed a strategic partnership with company Commonwealth Fusion Systems, which is racing to build a donut-shaped machine called a tokamak that could eventually generate 10 million times the energy of coal or natural gas, all without greenhouse gas emissions.

Fusion – replicating the power of the sun – has made major advances over the past few years. However, there’s still a big question on whether companies and governments can crack the thorniest problem: getting more energy out than you put into it and building the right machine to sustain that power.

AI companies are also seeking ways to make their own technology more efficient. Google, for example, has been expanding its ability to ramp up or down its operations depending on other users’ demand for power.

Big batteries that store wind and solar energy are another solution, since they can be used to supplement gas turbines. Hertz-Shargel said batteries are becoming a necessity for data centers: The way these facilities consume power can cause issues with electrical currents, which damages gas turbines and electric infrastructure. In these cases, batteries can act as a buffer between the data center and the grid to protect its infrastructure.

Hertz-Shargel said data center demand will be a “huge” boon for the battery storage industry, especially for companies working on future battery technology. The big spending on data centers provides a reliable revenue stream that the “long duration storage industry really needs,” he said.

Despite the hurdles to getting more power, others are more optimistic. Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis told a CNBC podcast earlier this year that he believes AI will end up helping solve its own energy crises.
“I think there are multiple breakthroughs that AI could come up with and help us come up with that would help with the energy situation,” he said.",CNN

Fri, 24 Apr 2026 07:00:00 GMT,Can Texas' power grid handle the meteoric rise of AI data centers?,"HOUSTON - Last week, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) presented a six-year forecast of how much power demand they expect in the near future. When the numbers showed a quadrupled peak demand by 2032, the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) sent them back to the drawing board.

As they work to compile a more desirable plan for the future, a look at what they expect to happen in Texas can still attempt to answer the question of how data centers might change the state's electricity landscape.
ERCOT load forecast
By the numbers:

In the presentation given on Friday, ERCOT's first slate of numbers gives a more conservative estimate of use that's based solely on ""core components,"" excluding projected large (75 megawatts or more) and medium (25–74.9 MW) loads on their radar. As a start, they imagine this summer may see a peak demand of 90,500 to 98,000 MW, exceeding the highest recorded peak of 85,508 MW in summer 2023.

By 2032, again ignoring new loads that haven't yet been built, they expect the peak to grow by increments of a few thousand MW per year until a high of around 111,000. This is based on economic growth, EV and PV adoption, crypto growth in existing mining facilities, and large loads that are already operational.
ERCOT load forecast + data centers

The chart that caused the PUCT to balk, however, includes the previously omitted large and medium loads on the horizon. The bars below represent the first graph along with projects that have been requested but have not yet been built.
By the numbers:

According to these numbers, the demand on the grid could more than double within two years. Two years after that, it would be tripled. By 2032, Texas could see a peak demand of more than 367,000 MW; over quadruple what the state expects to see this summer.
As shown in the next graph, the largest contributors to these potential spikes would be non-crypto data centers.
Planned data center loads
By the numbers:

Of that quadrupled number in 2032, more than 235,000 MW are expected to be taken up by data centers. Another chart in the presentation gives a look at the 2025 version of submitted plans versus those submitted in 2026.
ERCOT to change forecast

After presenting these predictions, the PUCT told ERCOT to draft a more reasonable look at the future of the state's power demand. Even before the presentation, the energy council's president and CEO, Pablo Vegas, said in a statement that the numbers were likely an overestimate.
What they're saying:

Texas is experiencing exceptional growth and development, which is reshaping how large load demand is identified, verified, and incorporated into long-term planning,"" said Vegas on April 15. ""As a result of a changing landscape, we believe this forecast to be higher than expected future load growth. We look forward to working with the PUCT on potential adjustments to refine how ERCOT ascertains the most accurate information for load forecasting and ensuring the system reliably and efficiently serves Texans.""

On the side of the PUCT, they expect any changes to the predictions to be in alignment with developing state legislation, keeping large loads within the bounds of the grid's capacity and maintaining the reliability of the system.

The PUCT and ERCOT continue to implement Senate Bill 6, creating the necessary rules and procedures to ensure new large power users can connect to the ERCOT grid, while maintaining grid reliability and ensuring residential consumers aren’t footing the bill for new infrastructure costs,"" a Friday statement from the commission says in part.
How the Texas grid has improved
Big picture view:

Along with their promise for continued grid trustworthiness, the PUCT said in an email to FOX Local that the state's electricity system is ""more reliable than it has ever been,"" which is due to changes they and ERCOT have made since the deadly winter storm of 2021.

Among those changes, their statement says, are better weatherization, lower price caps, generator capacity improvements, better reliability standards, updated data systems and response protocol, and voter-approved funding for more energy production.
AI data centers on the rise
Dig deeper:

While ERCOT has been told to revise their forecast, the fact remains that their initial stab at the project was based on requests for new large-scale projects that will have to rely on the same grid as Texas' nearly 32 million residents. If the numbers are even close to accurate, the taxpayers who fund maintenance and upgrades to the grid can expect some level of increased demand in coming years.

To date, there are over 400 data centers either operating, under construction or in the planning stages in Texas. The state is set to overtake Virginia as the U.S. leader in data centers within the decade. In recent months, Google announced a $40 billion data center investment in Texas, and OpenAI and Oracle have launched projects as well. The final demands on the grid these and similar projects will produce are not yet known.
How it affects your wallet
Why you should care:

There's a chance that the taxpayer could avoid bearing all the costs of meeting those demands. As a boom in data center construction looms on the horizon, there are plans in the works to make those centers grid partners rather than power drains.

President Donald Trump signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge in March, which requires hyperscalers and AI companies to build, bring, or buy all the energy needed for building and operating data centers. This pledge, however, operates as a voluntary agreement between companies and utility systems, which can be backed out of. A federally enforceable version of such a requirement could be required down the road to keep taxpayers off the hook for infrastructure expansion.

Additionally, renewable energy and alternative power generation, such as gas-fired plants and nuclear power, could be a key component in bolstering the grid as demand rises. FOX Local has reached out to energy leaders with plans for such projects to see how ERCOT's projections could affect their outlook, but they had not responded by the time of publishing.
The bottom line:

At the end of the day, the future of Texas' grid, infrastructure and data center landscape is largely theoretical and dependent on changes to policy and cooperation between massive, profit-driven entities as the situation develops. Once ERCOT returns with their amended plans, the extent to how much adaptation will be required will become clearer.
The Source: Information in this article comes from ERCOT, the Public Utility Commission of Texas, and previous FOX Local coverage.",FOX 26 Houston

Sat, 25 Apr 2026 07:00:00 GMT,Western grid power operator now has coal-burning Craig Unit 1 running,"A reluctant Tri-State Generation and Transmission is now burning coal and sending electricity out onto the grid from its Craig Unit 1, after the Western power grid authority said potential for outages at other plants meant the northwestern Colorado power is needed to balance regional resources.

Tue, 28 Apr 2026 07:00:00 GMT,Fusion energy could soon be joining the U.S. power grid,"On Tuesday a fusion energy start-up announced that it has applied to join a U.S. power grid—a first that could one day see households and businesses powered by nuclear fusion.

The application process requires a potential energy provider to provide extensive technical information to the grid operator, including descriptions of the planned fuel type. It’s a process that mimics the nuclear reactions in the sun, including the particles involved: isotopes of hydrogen called deuterium and tritium. The promise of the device is that a fusion reaction could feasibly generate limitless clean energy. That energy, in the form of heat, is used to boil water into steam, which then pushes a turbine to produce electricity.*

Just before 2:00 p.m., they strapped the replacement metal pole to the boom on their truck and hoisted it vertically into the air.

Setting a new pole is an act of both muscularity and balletic precision, but for experienced linemen, it’s a typical task. The new pole must be held steady at the bottom while an operator in the truck uses a claw on the end of the boom to maneuver it into a waiting hole. When done right, linemen can replace multiple utility poles in a day, but things in Seminole didn’t go as planned: When the boom operator attempted to grab the pole with the claw, he bumped against it instead, causing the top of the pole to accidentally make contact with the high-voltage transmission lines running overhead.

The explosion that followed was so violent it lit the earth itself on fire. Sixty-nine thousand volts, enough to feed the substation, powering entire neighborhoods, diverted from the wire into the new pole and rocketed toward the ground. In the current’s way stood Justin Bryan, a thirty-year-old father and music director at his local church, who was balancing the pole from below. The current ripped through Bryan’s body, killing him. It continued flowing into the ground around the truck, causing the grassy field to burst into flames, smoke billowing skyward. Two other linemen, Jefferey Busch and Matthew Waldrop, fathers in their late twenties and early thirties, were also in contact with the pole and were left crawling on the charred earth, horrifically burned but alive. Bystanders could do little to help; so long as the wires remained energized, electricity could still arc and flow anywhere in the vicinity.

I first saw an eyewitness video of the accident’s horrific aftermath this past December, not long after I had arrived at the headquarters of Pack Power Services, a utility-services company nestled among the horse farms of Ohio Amish country. Work had been slow; a thin dusting of snow coated the few dozen bucket trucks and pickups in the lot outside the company’s warehouse.

When I started reporting on the lives of linemen late last year, I quickly discovered that although linemen are on the front lines of maintaining the power grid—our connection to medical care, drinking water, cell phones, the Internet, emergency services, lights, heat, you name it—no one knows much about them. Most people assumed I was writing about football. But the people who did know what a lineman was kept telling me to talk to the same person: Pack Power’s owner, Jerry Pack. Colleagues told me that he was the quintessential lineman—an Army vet and a biker; rough around the edges, sure, but loyal to a fault. But he was also more than an archetype. Jerry had helped revolutionize the trade and ridden its ups and downs for years.

When I got in touch, Jerry, who looks a bit like the actor Brendan Gleeson if Brendan Gleeson had a graying ZZ Top beard and tattoos down his forearms, invited me to come visit on a Thursday—“That’s when we drink,” he said—and greeted me at the warehouse door with a lit Marlboro Red between his fingers. He had also invited a few other linemen with stories to tell, including Nick Mansfield, from East Texas, who quickly pulled me aside and asked if I wanted to see the “real shit” about being a lineman. He pulled his cell phone from his pocket and hit play on a copy of the Seminole video. I lasted only a few seconds before I had to look away.

Nick, who met Jerry years ago on the job and remains one of his closest friends, is a lineman’s lineman. He’s burly and bearded and wears a chain around his neck that, at first glance, appears to be a traditional Christ on the cross but isn’t Jesus at all. Rather, it’s a lineman climbing a utility pole. While the incident in Seminole was barely more than a blip in the local news, he told me linemen across the country had seen the video. There’s an old expression, he said: “Telegraph, telephone, tell a lineman.” Word travels fast in the industry, and the industry, lately, had heard too many stories like this. A lineman dies on the job on average once every two weeks, ranking it among the deadliest professions in America.

While Jerry and Nick showed me around the warehouse, we discussed the incident in Seminole. The Pinellas County Sheriff’s Office investigated and determined it was an accident, while OSHA recently levied $49,650 in penalties, which is being contested by the contractor hired by the utility company, Duke Energy. But as the video made its way from the jobsite to the union hall to TikTok, linemen in the comments section became fixated on the fact that the transmission line was energized during the work. Jerry and Nick told me that they would have demanded the utility de-energize the lines before getting started, a precaution that would have stopped all the meters in all the homes and businesses downstream of the substation from spinning—and from generating revenue. (When contacted about the details of the incident, Duke Energy replied with this statement: “The safety of our employees, contractors and customers remains Duke Energy’s highest priority, and we continue to cooperate fully with the ongoing investigation process.”)

Jerry understood, all too well, why so many linemen who saw the video scrutinized the safety practices that were in place. The men in Seminole had been doing what’s called “blue sky” work, regular repair and maintenance of the power grid. But the industry’s relentless push toward high speed and low cost were most evident in the niche kind of linework that Jerry specialized in: storm chasing.

In this run-and-gun model of linework, independent crews show up whenever and wherever they are needed to get the power back on after hurricanes, blizzards, and wildfires. Multiple linemen described the storm-chasing world to me as the “Wild West,” a place where the allure of big money attracted roguish personalities. For years, the living was good, great even, but to hear Jerry and Nick tell it, the frontier was closing. America’s electrical grid was becoming more critical to daily life than ever, and the opportunity to rake in profits had attracted middleman contractors and private-equity investment. For the storm chasers, that meant pressure to perform ratcheting ever higher, and their livelihoods coming under threat as the incentives to do whatever it took to secure contracts—aboveboard or otherwise—grew stronger. For the rest of us? It meant the future of the grid itself was at stake.

As the sun went down, the three of us drove the few minutes to Jerry’s ranch house, where we settled in around the kitchen table. Jerry’s girlfriend, Rita, who had already set out foil trays filled with pigs in a blanket and chicken wings on the stovetop, offered us pint glasses of vodka and cranberry juice. I asked Jerry when things started to change. “About ten years ago,” he said as he filled a paper plate with wings. “Irma was the fire under my ass.”

In 2017, Jerry was pulling into his driveway after work one day when he discovered his then-wife, Sally, waiting in the doorway in tears. “It’s cancer,” she told him. Her doctor had just called with the test results they’d been waiting for. Over the previous eighteen years, Jerry had worked his way up from an apprenticeship to doing blue-sky work at a substation as a contractor for a local utility. It was a good job with a regular schedule. Sally’s diagnosis changed everything. He’d need to be available to drive her to treatment and support her when she got home. He decided on the spot to drag up—quit without notice, in lineman-speak—and take to the road. “I’ll just storm-chase,” he told her. At the time, most power-restoration efforts were handled by mutual-aid agreements between utilities. If a hurricane hit Florida, a utility company in North Carolina might send some crews to help, understanding that Florida would return the favor if needed. A few large private energy companies had their own crews. Jerry started putting in calls.

If linework is the Wild West, storm chasers are the outlaws of the bunch. They’re the guys lauded as heroes on local-news broadcasts for restoring power after natural disasters, but among their ranks you can find all kinds, from drug-addled ex-felons to former lawyers and everything in between. Some storm chasers, affectionately known as tramps, essentially live on the road full-time, traveling the country in RVs or tricked-out pickup trucks, going wherever they’re needed. They keep two drag bags packed at all times: one for their gear—harnesses, hard hats, and boot spikes for climbing utility poles—and the other stuffed with a week’s worth of clothes. Walker Pettis, a tramp from Washington, told me he’s moved thirty times in the past five years.

No sooner had Jerry decided to join their ranks than the strongest hurricane in recent memory began intensifying in the southern Atlantic. The meteorologists called it Irma. “THIS IS AS REAL AS IT GETS,” wrote the National Weather Service in a tweet the night before Irma struck. Residents were urged to flee. In the largest exodus in American history, some seven million Floridians got in their cars and drove north, leaving their homes, businesses, and belongings behind.

Jerry, on the other hand, jumped in a truck and headed south toward Miami, amid a caravan of vehicles carrying linemen from across the country. He had gotten a call from an acquaintance asking if he could lead a crew. At his day job before storms, Jerry usually ran with four other guys; in Florida, he’d be in charge of 120. “I was scared to fucking death, dude,” he said.

In Miami, Jerry and his crew holed up in a hotel and watched through the windows as Irma transformed the world around them: waves of water breaching the Miami River seawall, palm trees blown horizontal in the gale, alligators wandering suburban sidewalks. Nearly two thirds of the state was left without power. Some sixty thousand linemen had descended on the state, and the utility companies scrambled to get organized. The linemen were happy to wait; they were getting paid whether they left the hotel or not. Chaos is cash, as linemen like to say, and Irma had brought the chaos.

President Trump described the response as “the largest assemblage of human beings ever in one area for power.” Linemen faced floodwaters, live wires dangling amid the trees, and bird dogs from the utility companies—the office workers tasked with directing crews to their next work site—pressuring them to work on high-voltage lines in gusts of wind and rain. While they moved from one downed pole or blown-out transformer to the next, Jerry and his crew were approached by elderly couples desperate for help and by countless residents demanding to have their TVs turned back on. In a little over a week, the linemen had fully restored power in a state of twenty million people. Public officials hailed them as heroes.
Jerry didn’t feel like a hero until he deposited his paycheck. His stress finally abated. “Don’t sweat it,” he told Sally. “We’re all set.”

Irma changed everything for Jerry, and it changed everything for linemen. The traditional mutual-aid model was effective, but it could be slow. Pack Power, which Jerry started after returning from Irma, was one of the country’s first linemen-owned businesses to offer something different: rapid response. Jerry’s guys could be sent anywhere they were needed at a moment’s notice. Within a few years, a post-Irma surge of these kinds of outfits had revolutionized the industry. “Years ago, there were no companies that just did storm work,” said a stockbroker-turned-lineman who left what he described as the “scumbag business” of Wall Street and now runs a storm-recovery business on the East Coast. “Today, I’d only be guessing, but I would say there’s probably close to between six hundred to a thousand companies that do just that.”

After we’d been talking for an hour, Randy Wolfe slipped into the kitchen. A slight, quiet guy in his early forties who lived nearby, he sat down on a kitchen stool and pulled a Modelo from some hidden recess of his lime-yellow reflective work jacket. Randy epitomized the stormchasing lineman of the post-Irma era, who were in control of their schedules and making fortunes unthinkable to their blue-sky brethren. His taste in beer may be lowbrow, but he owns a collection of high-end sports cars, including a C5 Corvette and a Lotus Elise. More than once, the quiet roads around Jerry’s house had been lit up by wailing sirens and flashing lights as Randy outran the cops in one of his supercars.
Randy described the gaps between jobs like this: “I pick a car and I go to the lake all day. If the phone rings, fine. If it don’t ring, fantastic.”
For this new generation of linemen, storm-chasing became as much a lifestyle as a livelihood, built on the twin pillars of money and freedom. “We’re like modern-day pirates,” said Nick.

At first, all Jerry had wanted was the freedom to bring Sally to her oncology appointments in Chicago without worrying about sick days or PTO. But once the money started rolling in, he bought a few Porsches and some rental properties and expanded his fleet of bucket trucks. The indoor hot tub he installed at his house was so big he had to build a new room to go around it.

In order to maintain this newfound abundance, storm chasers relied on a steady stream of what’s known in the business as Good Storms. What exactly makes a Good Storm is up for debate, though time is the obvious answer. A Good Storm lasts a couple weeks at least. The longest can go on for a month or more. For linemen working sixteen-hour days, seven days a week, a Good Storm can yield a paycheck on par with the average American annual salary. Jerry told me that during Irma—one of the best storms in recent memory—the most experienced guys on his crew, which was unionized, were being paid around $150 an hour, double or even triple the going rate back home. That’s $16,800 a week, not including food, travel, and a place to sleep. Though most linemen will proudly recount stories of residents thanking them for getting their power back on after a disaster, it’s clear they’re not in it for the goodwill alone. “This isn’t a humanitarian effort,” as one lineman told me. Nick’s been doing it for so long he now refers to the Weather Channel as “the Money Channel.” Linemen have been known to quit salaried positions without notice just to join a single storm roster during hurricane season.

This wayward streak has long been associated with linework. Nick’s “line dad”—his mentor—told him that the roots of the linemen’s renegade spirit can be found in the Vietnam vets who returned from the war and joined the ranks because they felt out of place in society. But the storm-chasing lifestyle brought it to new heights. After driving long hours in caravans of bucket trucks, linemen ride out storms everywhere from empty hotel rooms to hammocks in the backs of their trucks to military-style tent-and-cot setups known as “man camps.” These overnights offer the chance for a lineman’s worst instincts to flourish—hard drinking, affairs with local women dubbed “bucket bunnies,” even crime. Linemen on storm have been accused of everything from felony assault to trafficking drug shipments in their trucks. “There is a culture in linework that is seedy, romanticized, drug ridden,” the former stockbroker said. “There’s a lot of guys that are looking for the next high.” Nick once had a crewmate who found himself face-to-face with an angry pimp after unceremoniously kicking a sex worker out of his hotel room in the middle of the night. A fight ensued and the pimp ended up both beaten up and under arrest. “The lineman was at work at seven in the fucking morning,” Nick recalled.

And yet, despite all the potential for misadventure, the shared unpleasantness of sleepless nights and long waits for food at the mess tent had a way of turning colleagues into comrades. “We meet guys one time,” said Nick, “work a storm for a week, and you become lifelong friends.” Nick’s been sober for half a year now, and all night Jerry subtly topped him off with water, not wanting him to stare at an empty glass while we downed our cocktails. Linework was simply too dangerous to do anything but have each other’s back, Jerry told me. “Your ego can’t get in that.” Randy lit up describing how a crowd of linemen had gathered in awe and respect when he and his father ran into each other on storm and set a utility pole together. “It was one of the coolest things I’ve ever been a part of,” he said, pulling another Modelo from his vest. He’d keep drinking them all night.

They were a merry band in those days. They saw themselves as something like outlaws, because they’d found a way to make money hand over fist living an itinerant, rambunctious lifestyle that suited them. They were getting away with something. But the hard-partying, carefree life was about to get a lot harder. “Those days are about gone,” Jerry said, wistfully. Someone with an even better way to turn chaos into cash was riding into town.

Jaradda Sparks sensed an opportunity. The forward-thinking lineman from Alabama saw more and more storm chasers following Jerry in opening their own companies. He also saw utilities struggling to manage them. He went straight to the utility companies and promised to save them time and money by aggregating the services of hundreds of smaller storm-chasing companies under the umbrella of his own, Sparks Energy. If a storm hit, a power company only had to make one call, to Sparks, to secure the services of thousands of linemen spread out across the country. No more shopping or logistics; Sparks was a one-stop shop. He charged the utilities a hefty premium, but they were clearly willing to pay: By 2019, he had made enough money to open his own livestock ranch, specializing in breeding “top-caliber bucking bulls” for the rodeo circuit.

This new aggregator model initially had a beneficial trickle-down effect. Sparks declined to speak with me for this article, but I heard from many linemen that while his approach was designed to cater to utilities, it also funneled jobs to storm chasers in his network, who could work dozens of storms a year without the legwork of going out and bidding for new business. Jerry grossed $15 million one of the years he worked under Sparks as a subcontractor.

But the model was so successful that aggregators soon multiplied, just as the storm-chasing outfits once had, creating competition that made life harder for guys like Jerry. In order to lock in higher premiums from utility companies, aggregators tried to corner the market, securing ironclad contracts that ensured utilities would work only with them. Independent companies found it increasingly challenging to land contracts of their own.

In intervening years, the industry took on a new shape. There was still a ton of money to be made, but now there was a lot more competition, a new layer of middlemen, and more complicated contracts. This environment cut into the bottom lines of companies like Pack Power. It also opened the door to bad actors. None of the dozen active linemen I spoke to for this story were willing to go on the record about corruption in the industry, but they’ve worked all over the country and nearly all had stories. One storm chaser told me a company he’d worked for hauled broken-down bucket trucks on wreckers to storms because they were being paid per truck, even if the trucks sat in a parking lot unused. Another lineman told me he had been sent out on a storm crew without the proper tools or dielectric testing to make sure the trucks were insulated in case of an accident. When the crews came back an hour later, unable to work, he still got paid. Less visible backroom deals were also in play. One storm-company owner told me explicitly that he paid $15,000 for an executive at a power company to go on an overseas trip in exchange for better work contracts, only for the executive to ghost him once he had returned. The cutthroat competition in the industry incentivized these tactics, and the problems were perpetuated when word, inevitably, got out. Telegraph, telephone, tell a lineman.

These shifting practices may also have put lives at risk. At least one lineman I spoke to who asked not to be named told me that some aggregators were known for hiring “guys who weren’t qualified to do the work and going out with trucks that didn’t have any tooling on them.”

Jerry’s business suddenly began to suffer. After a couple of years in the black, he found that he was getting fewer calls from aggregators. He told me that inexperienced, nonunion linemen were willing to work for less money per hour than his guys, brothers in the IBEW. Then it stopped being standard for aggregators to pay linemen for mobilization and travel days, forcing those costs to come out of Jerry’s bottom line instead.

All this, and many questioned whether the aggregator model was actually saving anyone any money. Average electricity prices are up more than 30 percent across the country in the last five years alone. Are the changes in linework the reason why? It’s hard to say for certain—but it certainly hasn’t helped.

Looking back, the storm chasers should have known the end of their era was near when the bucket bunnies broke the Internet. In 2022, a Florida TikToker revealed that in the weeks following Hurricane Ian, her Tinder account had become overrun with linemen heading to the Sunshine State for storm work. “Everyone saying pray for Florida but this is our tinder right now,” she wrote before the reel revealed that, extensive storm damage aside, things in the state maybe weren’t so bad: There was a stream of handsome, well-paid linemen in town looking for dates. Other users followed suit, posting videos of linemen mobilizing for work outside hotels and in parking lots. Then the “linewives,” the married partners of linemen, arrived, posting their own TikToks railing against the bucket bunnies who were out to steal their men.

The melodrama was hugely popular. The bucket-bunny trend lasted for months and was viewed nearly three billion times, landing it just behind the Ice Bucket Challenge as one of the most popular memes of the past few years. It spawned merchandise; online commenters begged for a reality-TV show.

The linemen, however, were unenthused. As word got out about how much money they were making, sleeping with women while on storm became a lot less carefree. Nick, in his inimitable way, took the opportunity to explain the other three T’s of linework: “You buy your girl new teeth, new tits, and a brand-new Tahoe, before she walks out on you,” he said. Some apprentices, he told me, stopped letting women know they were linemen. Social media had transformed bucket bunnies, at one time the consummate example of the linemen’s freewheeling lifestyle, into a new kind of peril, one that could lead to divorce or something even worse: child support.
Of course, if enough money was flying around that bucket bunnies could sniff it out, it was only a matter of time before the real bloodhounds showed up: Wall Street.

In the past few years alone, high-powered private-equity firms like BlackRock and Blackstone have found ways to get their cut. Attracted by the potential for a huge, data-center-driven increase in energy, they’ve spent billions buying up major utility providers in places like Minnesota, Indiana, New Mexico, and abroad. According to one count, some 150 million customers in the U. S. now rely on utilities funded at least in part by private-equity money. Under the PE model, buying into the companies that service those utilities is simply another layer of vertical integration to leverage. Just last year, Apollo Global Management spent roughly $2 billion to acquire a stake in PowerGrid Services, a prominent grid-repair and maintenance company founded by a former lineman in 2016.

Investments like these are touted as necessary to improve the grid’s infrastructure. Last July, BlackRock’s CEO, Larry Fink, said as much in an interview on CNBC. “We believe that there’s a need for trillions of dollars investing in infrastructure related to our power grids, AI, the whole digitization of the economy,” said Fink. But how big money’s incursion into the grid will affect both linemen and ratepayers is less clear. According to industry studies, the average length of power outages in 2025 was 40 percent longer than in the three years prior. Part of that is down to the increasing severity and frequency of the storms themselves. But an experienced workforce of linemen is essential to the recovery effort. And for them, private equity has been even worse than for customers. In the last two years alone, nonunion linemen have seen pay shrink, while call times to mobilize for storms have shortened from a few days to a few hours. “In the beginning of my storm-chasing career,” Jerry explained, “you had a reasonable time to get there. See the lady, get packed up, take her out to eat. Get on a plane the next day.” Now, he continued, “I have to have guys at the shop ready to leave at all times.” This sometimes means defying DOT rules limiting the number of hours bucket-truck drivers can spend on the road. Once they’ve arrived, the already fatigued linemen are still expected to work sixteen-hour days, seven days a week, until the job is done.

So far, linemen have been spared their Perfect Storm moment; there’s no mass tragedy that defines the trade. Instead, the specter of death arrives in a slow, steady cadence. In April of last year, a lineman was killed in Tennessee when his truck overturned into floodwaters; a few weeks later, four linemen were killed in North Carolina when a city dump truck crashed into their work site; in May, a falling tree in Alabama killed a lineman where he stood; in July, a lineman was electrocuted a few miles from where the Seminole tragedy unfolded a month later; in October, a hit-and-run; November, another electrocution, this time in Louisville. A number of fatal incidents show how pressure to cut corners and use junior crews can make the job even more perilous. In recent years, OSHA has assessed penalties of more than $40,000 and claimed that the lack of proper safety precautions led to at least two separate fatal incidents. In one, an electric company “failed to meet their responsibility to ensure a safe and healthful workplace and ensure the proper supervision of new workers.” That incident, in Alabama, resulted in the death of two nineteen-year-old apprentices. In the other, in Miami, a contractor “failed to use required safeguards before starting work,” and a thirty-two-year-old lineman died.

Earlier in the evening, I had asked Jerry about the worst accident he had ever seen. He sighed and slumped slightly in his chair; Nick shot me a glance. Don’t go there. But when I brought it up again later, I got a different response: indignation at how the blame for injuries and deaths always seemed to fall at the feet of the linemen themselves, as opposed to, say, contractors or utility companies pressuring crews to work despite safety concerns. “Doesn’t matter what happens, who dies,” Nick said. “The problem can never get back to the power company.”

Despite the contested fine levied by OSHA in the Seminole incident, the families of all three victims have had to fend for themselves, starting GoFundMe campaigns to help cover the cost of their recovery. It’s something Anne-Marie Olivieri, a linewife, has seen all too often. She founded the LineLife Foundation to help raise money for linemen killed on the job and as part of her effort tracks every injury and death she can, compiling lists and sharing them among linemen and their families. According to her, the tallies are rarely complete. “A lot of these are swept under the rug or they don’t get reported,” she told me. “There’s been times where I’ve actually gotten pictures of the accident and the company has threatened me.” Wary of a lawsuit, she declined to discuss the particulars, but her experience informs a fear among linemen that in this new private-equity world, shareholder profit, not outage times or lineman safety, will be the new benchmark for success.
Nick, indelibly, described how linemen feel. After an accident, he said, “they’ll post your job before they post your obituary.”

Around 11:00 p.m., Jerry pushed back from the kitchen table, stood up, and announced it was time to go to the hot-tub room. In there, Nick lit up a cigar while Jerry showed me his collection of Donald Trump–styled rubber duckies and bottles of Pappy Van Winkle bourbon. Like the Vietnam vets who had found a home in linework before him, Jerry had spun a decent day job into his own American dream: freedom, money, and the open road. But it was fleeting. The salad days of $15 million in gross are long gone.

So far, Jerry is uninterested in cashing in on the private-equity money-go-round, partly, it seems, due to pride. Money and freedom, both valuable things, aren’t quite the same. “There was a time when I had to roll my own fucking cigarettes,” he told me. “I built this, I made every fucking bit of this.” He’d rather hand off Pack Power Services to his kids than to a Wall Street firm. Chris, his eldest son, is already in a leadership role, handling much of the company’s day-to-day responsibilities, including storm work. PJ, another son, is the in-house mechanic. Jerry’s daughter stands to inherit his rental properties. And while he and Sally, recovered from cancer, split up a few years ago, she lives just a few minutes away in a house Jerry says he paid for.

This future is dependent on whether or not the company survives. Like nearly all the other businesses started by former linemen whose owners I spoke to, the injection of big money into the industry has made it difficult for Pack Power to compete. In the good ol’ days, Jerry had millions in the bank and no debt. “Now I’ve got fifty grand in the bank and I’m two million in the hole,” he told me.

Jerry still has the lineman’s hustle in his blood. He’s working on a deal to help the FAA modernize the infrastructure at a nearby airport. And there’s this other thing. “As soon as I saw Russia invading Ukraine, I knew we, as the United States, were going to be rebuilding their power grid,” he told me. “I’d love to be on that.” I didn’t know how seriously to take him, considering we were surrounded by empty beer cans and a haze of cigar and cigarette smoke. But as it turns out, Jerry had in fact spent much of the past year developing plans with a partner in the UK to join the international effort to rebuild Ukraine’s power grid, whenever that day comes.

It was nearing midnight when I left Jerry’s, the image of a crew of American linemen stepping off a plane in postwar Kyiv, just as they’d rushed into California after a wildfire or Florida after Irma, running through my head. The Wild West had been tamed, so they’d have to go find a new frontier. Outside, it was dark; there weren’t many streetlights in the neighborhood. But as I drove past the Pack Power warehouse on the way to my hotel, it was a different sight that stirred something in me: a long row of bucket trucks parked in the lot out front, ready and waiting for the next job, still coated in snow but illuminated under the warehouse lights.",Esquire
